---
title: "Sensitivity Analysis, Scenario Analysis, and Break-Even Analysis"
output: pdf_document
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE)
source("../examples/7_1.R")
table_7_2 <- read.csv("../data/table_7_2.csv")
scenarios <- colnames(table_7_2)[-1]
vars <- table_7_2$variable
base <- as.list(table_7_2$base)
names(base) <- vars
cash_flows <- lapply(table_7_2$variable, function(v) {
    sapply(table_7_2[table_7_2$variable == v, names(table_7_2)[-1]], function(x) {
        some_list <- modifyList(base, setNames(list(x), v))
        do.call(calc_cash_flows, some_list)
    })
})
names(cash_flows) <- vars
table_7_3 <- as.data.frame(bind_rows(lapply(names(cash_flows),
                              function(v) unlist(cash_flows[[v]]['npv',]))))
rownames(table_7_3) <- vars
```

The net present value technique is used to determine whether a project should
be accepted. If the project's NPV is positive, the project should be accepted.
Otherwise it should be rejected. When calculating the NPV, you need to
understand which variables matter the most and how varying them will affect the
NPV. Two ways of studying the effects of the variables on NPV are sensitivity
analysis and scenario analysis.

Sensitivity analysis allows you to vary one variable from a base case. The
advantage of this analysis is that you can observe how much impact a single
variable has on the NPV. The disadvantage to sensitivity analysis is that, in
the real world, most of the variables are related and vary together.

The beginning of the example starts with a breakdown of the cash flow forecasts
for Solar Electronics Corporation's Jet Engine: Base case.

| | Year 1 | Year 2-6 |
|:---|:---:|---:|
| Revenues                 | | `$6,000` |
| Variable costs           | | ` 3,000` |
| Fixed costs              | | ` 1,791` |
| Depreciation             | | `   300` |
| Pretax profit            | | `$  909` |
| Tax ($t_c$ = .34)        | | `   309` |
| Net profit               | | `$  600` |
| Cash flow                | | `$  900` |
| Initial investment costs | `$1,500` | |

This cash flow is estimated to be the same for the next five years. We can
calculate the NPV of the project using a 15 percent discount rate:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{NPV} &= -\$1{,}500 + \sum^{5}_{i=1}{\frac{\$900}{(1.15)^t}}\\
  &= -\$1{,}500 + \$900 \times \text{PVIA}(.15, 5)\\
  &= \$1{,}517
\end{aligned}
$$

Because the NPV is positive, we should accept the project. However, we should
check the underlying assumptions about revenues and costs.

## Revenues

The marketing department has projected the following annual sales for jet engines:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Sales} &= \text{SEC market share} \times \text{Market size}\\
3{,}000 &= .30 \times 10{,}000\\
\\
\text{revenues} &= \text{sales} \times \text{price}\\
\$6{,}000 \text{ million} &= 3{,}000 \times \$2 \text{ million}
\end{aligned}
$$

Revenue estimates depend on three assumptions:

1. Market share.
2. Size of jet engine market.
3. Price per engine.

## Costs

We divide costs into variable and fixed costs. Variable costs will vary with
the number of jet engines produced. Fixed costs are a flat annual rate
regardless of the number of jet engines produced. The engineering department
estimates costs:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{annual variable costs} &= \text{unit variable costs}
  \times \text{number of engines produced}\\
  \$3{,}000 \text{ million} &= \$1 \text{ million} \times 3{,}000\\
\\
\text{annual total costs} &= \text{annual variable costs} + \text{annual fixed costs}\\
\$4{,}791 \text{ million} &= \$3{,}000 \text{ million} + \$1{,}791 \text{ million}
\end{aligned}
$$

These are the expected or best estimates of the different parameters. We could
also produce optimistic and pessimistic forecasts for comparison.

| Variable | Pessimistic | Expected or Best | Optimistic |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| Market size (per year) | 5,000 | 10,000 | 20,000 |
| Market share           | 20\% | 30\% | 50\% |
| Price                  | \$1.9 million | \$2 million | \$2.2 million |
| Variable cost (per engine) | \$1.2 million | \$1 million | \$.8 million |
| Fixed cost (per year)  | \$1,891 million | \$1,791 million | \$1,741 million |
| Investment | \$1,900 million | \$1,500 million | \$1,000 million |

To conduct sensitivity analysis on the project, we would vary one of these
variables, and hold the other variables at their expected value.

For instance if we want to calculate the NPV for a pessimistic market size of 5,000:

```{r example}
ex1 <- unlist(cash_flows$market_size[,'pessimistic'])
sales         <- pretty(ex1['units'])
revenues      <- pretty(ex1['revenues']/1e6)
var_costs     <- pretty(ex1['var_costs']/1e6)
market_size   <- pretty(table_7_2[table_7_2$variable == 'market_size', 'pessimistic'])
market_share  <- table_7_2[table_7_2$variable == 'market_share', 'base']
total_cost    <- pretty(sum(ex1[c('var_costs', 'fixed_costs')])/1e6)
price         <- pretty(table_7_2[table_7_2$variable == 'price', 'base']/1e6)
fixed_cost    <- pretty(ex1['fixed_costs']/1e6)
```

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Sales} &= \text{SEC market share} \times \text{Market size}\\
`r sales` &= `r market_share` \times `r market_size`\\
\\
\text{revenues} &= \text{sales} \times \text{price}\\
\$`r revenues` \text{ million} &= `r sales` \times \$`r price` \text{ million}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{annual variable costs} &= \text{unit variable costs}
  \times \text{number of engines produced}\\
  \$`r var_costs` \text{ million} &= \$1 \text{ million} \times `r sales`\\
\\
\text{annual total costs} &= \text{annual variable costs} + \text{annual fixed costs}\\
\$`r total_cost` \text{ million} &= \$`r var_costs` \text{ million}
  + \$`r fixed_cost` \text{ million}
\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate the cash flows:

```{r ex1_cash_flows}
cf_vars <- c("revenues", "var_costs", "fixed_costs", "depreciation",
             "pretax", "tax", "net_profit", "cash_flow")
ex1_cash_flows <- as.data.frame(format(round(ex1[cf_vars]/1e6), big.mark=','))
rownames(ex1_cash_flows) <- c("Revenues", "Variable costs", "Fixed costs",
                              "Depreciation", "Pretax profit", "Tax (.34)",
                              "Net profit", "Cash flow")
knitr::kable(ex1_cash_flows,
             col.names = "Years 2-6",
             caption="Cash flows for pessimistic market size")
```

The negative taxes assume that SEC has other profitable operations.
Finally the NPV is
`r label_dollar(scale = 1e-6, accuracy = 1,
                suffix = " million")(round(ex1['npv']))`.

Running the sensitivity analysis for all variables we can generate the
following table:

```{r table_7_3}
rownames(table_7_3) <- c("Market size", "Market share", "Price",
                         "Variable cost", "Fixed cost", "Investment")

knitr::kable(round(table_7_3/1e6),
             caption = "NPV Calculations for the Solar Jet Engine Using Sensitivity Analysis",
             col.names = c("Pessimistic", "Expected", "Optimistic"))
```

The following table shows some sensitivity measures that can help in evaluating
the project.

```{r sensitivity_measures, echo=FALSE}
sensitivity_measures <- table_7_3 |>
    transmute(
        npv_range      = round((optimistic - pessimistic)/1e6),
        downside_ratio = round((base - pessimistic)/base, 2)) |>
    arrange(desc(npv_range))
colnames(sensitivity_measures) <- c("NPV Range", "Downside Ratio")
knitr::kable(sensitivity_measures, caption="Key Sensitivity Measures")
```

The range between pessimistic and optimistic outcomes for each variable is
useful to determine if we need more information about the input. For example,
in the table above, market size and market share have a very large range when
compared to the other NPV inputs. We may want to gather more information about
how these inputs are estimated. This can be done through market research or
test marketing.

The downside ratio is very useful in showing if a pessimistic outcome
would reverse the decision (ratio > 1), i.e. if the NPV can turn negative. This
will be a major factor in accept/reject decision making. The table shows that
market size and market share are the only two inputs that can make the NPV go
negative. Variable cost shows a near miss with a downside ratio of
`r sensitivity_measures['Variable cost', 'Downside Ratio']`. With a pessimistic
value, the NPV is only
`r label_dollar(scale=1e-6, accuracy=1,
                suffix=" million")(table_7_3['Variable cost', 'pessimistic'])`.
We may want to pay some attention to this input as well.

The market size and market share are clearly the most important inputs to the
NPV calculation and the decision to go ahead with full-scale production. Their
ranges are both more than twice the next-largest range and the downside ratios
for both show a significant risk for negative NPV.
